summary: Provides guidelines for registering and administering internationalized domain names in Chinese, Japanese and Korean. It deals with the problem of characters that look alike, and with deployment and administration issues beyond the IDNA protocol itself. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some letters in these languages look almost alike. Registries get advice on handling them so people are not tricked into the wrong website.

subtitle: How registries can reserve and group look-alike Chinese, Japanese and Korean domain labels so one owner holds them all.

tldr.problem: Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters often have several code points for one conceptual character, so look-alike domain labels can confuse users and be used for fraud, and IDNA alone does not address this.
tldr.mechanism: Each zone uses a per-language Language Variant Table to validate characters and generate variant labels. The labels are bundled into one atomic IDL Package: Preferred Variant Labels are activated and Character Variant Labels are reserved.
tldr.outcome: A single holder owns the label and all its variants, which reduces confusion. The result is only as good as the tables, and the guidelines are informational, not binding.

facts.label: Table columns
facts.value: 3 (Valid Code Point, Preferred Variant, Character Variant)

today: RFC 3743 is an Informational document from April 2004 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The IETF does not dictate registry policy, so these are guidelines that zones may adopt, adapt or ignore.

sections.title: Why CJK Domain Names Need Guidelines
sections.content:
Domain names were designed as identifiers without language context, but users now read them as words and names. For Chinese, Japanese and Korean (CJK), the same conceptual character can have several code points, which the RFC calls variants. Identical or similar characters with different code points raise the risk of confusion and fraud.

The IETF IDN Working Group produced IDNA (RFC 3490) with three supporting specifications: Stringprep (RFC 3454), Nameprep (RFC 3491) and Punycode (RFC 3492). Those handle encoding, mapping and matching. This document covers the administrative side: it gives zone administrators a framework, written by the Joint Engineering Team (JET) with members from CNNIC, TWNIC, KRNIC and JPNIC, and invites other language groups to write their own.

The RFC admits its limits. It cannot give universally accepted definitions of which variants are the same, and generated variants may not be meaningful words. The aim is to generate similar variants to be reserved, not meaningful words.
sections.plainLanguage: The same idea can be written with different but similar-looking characters. Tricksters could use a look-alike spelling to fool you, so the people who give out names need a plan.

sections.title: Key Terms and the Language Variant Table
sections.content:
The guidelines work one label at a time, so they speak of an IDL (Internationalized Domain Label) rather than IDN. They apply per zone, at any level of the hierarchy where CJK characters appear.

The heart of the scheme is a Language Variant Table, one per language permitted in a zone. Each row has three columns separated by semicolons: the Valid Code Point (only characters listed here may be registered for that language), the Preferred Variant (substitutions whose labels are normally registered, or activated), and the Character Variant (substitutions whose labels are reserved but not activated). A table begins with Reference lines and a Version line carrying a date as YYYYMMDD, and the syntax is given in ABNF. Who writes the tables, and how, is left to each registry.

Everything generated from one registration forms an IDL Package: the IDL, its associated languages, the version of the variant table, the reserved IDLs and the active IDLs (called Zone Variants).
sections.plainLanguage: For each language there is a list that says which characters are allowed and which ones look like them. Some look-alikes go on the real list of names, and others are just kept safe so nobody else can take them.

sections.title: Principles Behind the Guidelines
sections.content:
The text sets out principles that the registration steps implement. Where disputes arise it assumes first-come, first-served (FCFS) unless the zone has its own policy.

  • Each IDL should be associated with one or more languages. Leaving the language unspecified is NOT recommended.
  • Each IDL must be checked against the valid characters of its languages, and fails if any character is outside them.
  • Labels generated from Character Variants should be reserved so no one else can register them. They normally do not appear in the zone file and may not resolve unless the holder asks.
  • Labels generated from Preferred Variants should be resolvable, meaning they appear in the zone file.
  • The IDL and all its variants form one IDL Package, which is atomic: transfer and deletion apply to the whole package.

A zone may add its own rules to limit how many variant labels are reserved or registered, and such policy is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick the language, check every character is allowed, keep look-alikes safe for the same owner, and always hand the whole bundle to one person.

sections.title: Registration, Transfer and Activation
sections.content:
Registration follows eight steps. The label and its languages come in. The label is processed through Nameprep, and if that fails registration stops. Its availability is checked and any conflict goes to the zone's conflict policy. For each language the label is validated against the table, and the Preferred Variant Labels and Character Variant Labels are generated by substituting variant code points. The set of Zone Variants is all Preferred Variants plus the original label. The reserved set is the Character Variant Labels minus the Zone Variants. The IDL Package is created and the Zone Variants are converted with ToASCII and put in the zone file.

This can produce many labels: if two characters have three and two Preferred Variants, there are 12 variant labels.

Deleting an IDL Package frees all its labels again. A reserved variant can later be activated by moving it from the reserved set into the Zone Variants and into the zone file, and deactivated by the reverse. Changing a package's languages means deleting the package and registering anew, and when a variant table changes, existing packages must not be updated or affected.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry checks the name, makes a list of look-alikes, puts the most common ones on the real list, and keeps the rest for the same owner. Giving the name back means giving back the whole bundle.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC defines small example tables for zh-cn, zh-sg, zh-tw, ja and ko, and warns that they are not the actual tables and are not enough for real use; IANA keeps a voluntary registry of actual tables. It then walks through seven examples with labels spelled in Unicode code points.

Registering U+6E05 U+771F U+6559 for zh-cn, zh-sg and zh-tw (or ja alone) gives one Zone Variant, the label itself, plus seven reserved Character Variant Labels. Adding ko makes the registration invalid, because U+6E05 is not valid in the Korean table. Registering U+806F U+60F3 U+96C6 U+5718 for the three Chinese languages gives two Zone Variants, since zh-cn and zh-sg prefer U+8054 and U+56E2 while zh-tw keeps the original. A label written with the simplified form U+8054 fails when zh-tw is included, because U+8054 is not valid there.
sections.plainLanguage: If a name uses a character that one language does not allow, the whole signup is refused. If languages disagree about the best spelling, each preferred spelling gets its own live entry.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unrestricted use of non-ASCII characters in labels can confuse users and invite attacks, and for CJK an attacker can exploit different code points with identical or similar meaning. These guidelines offer a partial remedy: they block inappropriate characters from being registered and group variants so that only one owner can register them.

The protection is no better or worse than the per-zone, per-language tables. Mistakes in building a table may significantly reduce the quality of protection, and each table reflects a zone's own balance between risk and flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan helps stop look-alike tricks, but it is only as good as the lists of look-alike characters. A wrong list means weaker protection.
